question: How long does it take to refinish hardwood floors?
title: How Long Does Refinishing Hardwood Floors Take?
h1: How Many Days Should You Budget for Refinishing?
description: A full hardwood floor refinish takes 3-5 working days, but oil-based finish needs up to 30 days to cure - longer in Sarasota's humid months.
capsule: A full hardwood floor sand-and-refinish takes 3-5 working days from the first sanding pass to the last coat. Oil-based polyurethane needs up to 30 days to fully cure before furniture and rugs go back down, and Sarasota's summer humidity can stretch that further, so we build extra dry time into jobs scheduled June through September.

sections.h2: How long the actual work takes
sections.html:
Sanding, staining and coating a typical hardwood floor takes 3-5 working days on site. Day one is usually the coarse sanding pass that strips the old finish, followed by progressively finer grits until the wood surface is smooth and even. If you're changing stain color, that adds a day for staining and dry time before the first finish coat goes on. Most jobs get two to three coats of polyurethane, each needing several hours to dry before the next one, which is why the finish stage often takes longer than the sanding itself.

A larger home, a staircase in the mix, or rooms with a lot of cut-in edges around cabinets and built-ins can push a job toward the high end of that 3-5 day range. Our refinishing estimates note an expected day count up front, so you can plan around it rather than guessing.

StageTypical time
Coarse-to-fine sanding1-2 days
Staining (if changing color)1 day, plus dry time
Finish coats (2-3 coats)1-2 days
Full finish cure before rugs/furnitureUp to 30 days (oil-based)

sections.h2: Why cure time matters more than the days on your calendar
sections.html: The floor is walkable in socks within about a day of the last coat, but that's not the same as cured. Oil-based polyurethane needs up to 30 days to fully cure before it's ready for furniture, area rugs, and normal foot traffic in shoes. Water-based finishes generally cure faster, which is one reason we walk through finish options with customers who need the room back in use sooner - a rental turnover or a home going on the market can't always wait a full month. Felt pads under furniture legs and a rug pad chosen for hardwood, rather than a rubber-backed one that can trap moisture, both help protect a freshly finished floor once it's back in daily use.

sections.h2: How Florida humidity changes the timeline
sections.html: Finish cure time is a chemical reaction, and high ambient humidity slows it down - that's true of polyurethane generally, not something unique to Florida, but our summer humidity runs high enough for long enough that it's worth planning around. We recommend running air conditioning during and after the job to keep indoor humidity in a normal range, which helps the finish cure closer to the manufacturer's stated timeline instead of stretching well past it. A house left closed up with the AC off during a summer trip is one of the more common reasons we see a refinish take longer than the crew originally quoted. This is the same reason we run a slab moisture check as part of our subfloor and prep process before any new hardwood install, not just refinishing jobs.

sections.h2: Planning your schedule around a refinishing job
sections.html: Because the space isn't usable for normal living during sanding and isn't ready for rugs and furniture until the finish cures, most customers either stay elsewhere for the work week or refinish one section of the house at a time, closing that area off from pets and foot traffic until the finish is safe to walk on. If you're weighing a full sand-and-refinish against just patching a damaged area, ask us about a partial refinish or repair - it's faster but only makes sense when the color and sheen can be matched to the surrounding floor, and we'll tell you honestly at the walkthrough if a section is too worn for a clean match. Get a schedule built around your move-back-in date with a free estimate.

faqs.q: Can I walk on the floor the same day it's refinished?
faqs.a: You can usually walk in socks within about 24 hours of the last coat, but the finish isn't fully cured yet - avoid shoes, rugs and heavy furniture until the manufacturer's cure window has passed.

faqs.q: Does a water-based finish cure faster than oil-based?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Water-based polyurethane typically dries to the touch faster and often reaches a usable state sooner than oil-based, though full cure time still depends on the specific product and indoor humidity.

faqs.q: Can I speed up drying with fans or the AC?
faqs.a: Running the AC to control humidity helps more than fans alone, since it's ambient moisture in the air that slows the chemical cure, not just surface air movement.
